BAN-001.q: The opportunity cost of a decision is:
BAN-001.e: Opportunity cost isn't booked but is relevant to decisions.
o: The value of the best alternative forgone
BAN-001.x:
Basis: Decision analysis; economics (Buchanan – opportunity cost).
Analysis: Opportunity cost = the value of the best alternative forgone. It isn't booked (BAN-015) but is a relevant cost in decisions (BAN-002).
Distractors: B – explicit cash costs are only part; C is sunk cost (BAN-003); D – depreciation allocates past cost.
Note (investing): holding cash or a stock both carry opportunity cost – the expected return of the best alternative (deposits, another stock with a larger margin of safety).

BAN-002.q: A firm's warehouse could be rented out for VND 120 million/month. If used for a new project for 1 year, what is its opportunity cost (VND million)?
BAN-002.e: 120 × 12 = 1,440 million VND must be charged to the project.
BAN-002.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (opportunity cost of existing assets).
Working: Opportunity cost = 120 × 12 = VND 1,440 million.
Analysis: The warehouse is owned so no cash is spent, but using it forgoes 1,440 million of rent → include it in project costs (BAN-043). Ignoring it makes the project look more profitable than it is.

BAN-003.q: Sunk costs (spent and unrecoverable) shouldn't affect future decisions.
BAN-003.e: True. Only future costs and benefits that differ between options are relevant.
BAN-003.x:
Basis: Decision analysis; Thaler (1980) – the sunk cost fallacy.
Analysis: True. Sunk costs are spent and unrecoverable whatever is chosen → they don't differ across options → irrelevant. Only future costs and benefits that differ across options matter (BAN-004).
Note (investment psychology): 'winning back' a loss or holding because of the purchase price is the sunk cost fallacy – decide on current intrinsic value and prospects versus price.

BAN-004.q: A firm has spent VND 2 billion on product research. Completing needs 1 billion more; PV of expected inflows is 1.5 billion; stopping recovers nothing. The rational decision:
BAN-004.e: The 2 billion is sunk; compare 1.5 with 1.
o: Continue, since the incremental benefit of 1.5 exceeds the incremental cost of 1
Stop, since total cost of 3 exceeds 1.5
BAN-004.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (incremental analysis).
Working: Incremental benefit of continuing = PV 1.5 billion; incremental cost = 1 billion; net = 1.5 − 1 = +0.5 billion > 0 → continue. Stopping: 0 in, 0 out.
Analysis: The 2 billion spent is sunk – lost either way. Comparing the 3 billion total with 1.5 billion (option B) is the fallacy. The project as a whole loses 1.5 billion in accounting terms, but continuing beats stopping by 0.5 billion.
Distractors: B and C are driven by sunk cost; D – 'at any cost' is escalation of commitment (BAN-086).

BAN-005.q: A plant with idle capacity receives a special order for 1,000 units at VND 90 thousand each; variable cost 70 thousand; fixed costs unchanged. What is the incremental profit (VND million)?
BAN-005.x:
Basis: Management accounting – special order decisions (Horngren).
Working: Incremental profit = (price − variable cost) × units = (90 − 70) × 1,000 = 20,000 thousand = VND 20 million.
Analysis: With idle capacity and unchanged fixed costs → any price above variable cost adds profit, even below full cost. Also consider effects on regular customers' prices, anti-dumping rules, and whether capacity is taken from better orders (BAN-006).

BAN-006.q: If the plant is at full capacity, evaluating a special order must also include:
BAN-006.e: That is the opportunity cost of capacity.
o: Contribution lost from displaced regular sales
BAN-006.x:
Basis: Management accounting – opportunity cost of capacity.
Analysis: At full capacity, accepting a special order displaces regular sales → the lost contribution margin is an opportunity cost → add it to relevant costs. Accept only if the new order's contribution exceeds the contribution lost.
Distractors: B – unchanged company-wide fixed costs are irrelevant; C is sunk; D – old-machine depreciation isn't incremental.

BAN-007.q: Making a component: variable cost VND 45 thousand each; fixed costs avoidable by buying out total 50 million for 10,000 units. What is the relevant cost of making per unit (VND thousand)?
BAN-007.e: 45 + 50,000/10,000 = 50; at a purchase price of 48, buy (saving 2/unit), also weighing quality and supply risk.
BAN-007.x:
Basis: Management accounting – make-or-buy decisions.
Working: Relevant cost to make = variable cost + avoidable fixed cost per unit = 45 + 50,000,000 / 10,000 / 1,000 = 45 + 5 = VND 50 thousand per unit.
Analysis: Only avoidable fixed costs (gone if buying) count; unavoidable common costs are ignored (BAN-008). A purchase price < 50 makes buying cheaper, but weigh qualitative factors: quality, supply risk, technology secrecy, alternative uses of freed capacity.

BAN-008.q: Allocated common (unavoidable) fixed costs are relevant when deciding whether to drop a product line.
BAN-008.e: False. Unavoidable costs remain even if the product is dropped.
BAN-008.x:
Basis: Management accounting – product discontinuation (BAN-009).
Analysis: False. Allocated common fixed costs (head-office rent, executive pay) are unavoidable – they remain if the line is dropped and are just reallocated → irrelevant. Relevant items: contribution margin lost and avoidable fixed costs.

BAN-009.q: A product line has contribution 300, avoidable fixed costs 200, allocated common costs 150 (reported loss 50). If dropped, how does company profit change?
BAN-009.e: Lose 300 contribution, save 200 → profit falls 100; don't drop it.
BAN-009.x:
Basis: Management accounting – segment margin reporting.
Working: If dropped: lose contribution 300, save avoidable fixed costs 200 → company profit changes −300 + 200 = −100. The 150 common cost remains.
Analysis: The reported 'loss of 50' (300 − 200 − 150) misleads; segment margin = 300 − 200 = +100 > 0 → the line contributes 100 to common costs → don't drop it (unless a better use of resources exists).
Check: Current profit includes −50 from this line; after dropping, the full 150 common cost remains → a −100 difference ✓.

BAN-010.q: The marginal principle says an activity should expand until:
BAN-010.e: If MB > MC, expand; if MB < MC, cut back.
o: Total benefit is largest regardless of cost
BAN-010.x:
Basis: Microeconomics – marginal analysis.
Analysis: Expand an activity while marginal benefit (MB) > marginal cost (MC); contract when MB < MC; the optimum is MB = MC – where net benefit peaks. It applies to output, hiring (BAN-011), advertising and working hours.
Distractors: B ignores cost; C – minimum average cost doesn't maximise profit; D – maximum revenue ignores cost.

BAN-011.q: Hiring one more salesperson costs VND 25 million/month; expected extra gross margin is 30 million/month. What is the net monthly benefit (VND million)?
BAN-011.e: 30 − 25 = 5 > 0 → hire if the estimate is reliable.
BAN-011.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (marginal analysis).
Working: Net monthly benefit = incremental gross profit − cost = 30 − 25 = VND 5 million > 0 → hire (if estimates are reliable).
Analysis: Test the 30 million assumption: is it taken from existing staff (cannibalisation – BAN-077)? ramp-up time? extra management cost? A 5 million margin (≈ 17%) is thin → sensitive to forecast error.

BAN-012.q: Select ALL RELEVANT costs/benefits for a decision:
BAN-012.e: Depreciation of existing assets reflects a sunk cost.
o: Future costs that differ between options
BAN-012.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (relevant costing).
Analysis: Relevant items are future and differ across options: (A) future costs differing by option; (B) opportunity cost of resources used (BAN-002); (C) incremental revenue; (D) avoidable fixed costs (BAN-007).
Distractors: (E) Depreciation of machines already bought allocates sunk cost – irrelevant; though future depreciation tax shields matter in project appraisal (BAN-050).

BAN-013.q: Machine hours are scarce. Product A: contribution 60/unit, 3 machine hours; B: 40/unit, 1 hour. What is B's contribution per machine hour?
BAN-013.e: B: 40/1 = 40 > A: 60/3 = 20 → prioritise B despite lower unit contribution.
BAN-013.x:
Basis: Management accounting – limiting factors.
Working: B: 40 / 1 = 40 per machine hour; A: 60 / 3 = 20 per machine hour.
Analysis: With scarce machine hours, each hour on B earns 40 versus 20 on A → prioritise B despite its lower unit contribution (BAN-014). Make B up to market demand, then use remaining hours for A.

BAN-014.q: With one limiting resource, a firm should prioritise the product with:
BAN-014.e: With several constraints, use linear programming.
o: The highest contribution per unit of the scarce resource
BAN-014.x:
Basis: Management accounting – limiting factors.
Analysis: With one constraint, rank products by contribution per unit of the scarce resource (BAN-013) – maximising total contribution from limited capacity. With several constraints at once (machine hours, materials, demand) → linear programming.
Distractors: B, C and D ignore scarce-resource consumption.
Note (capital management): the same applies to allocating limited capital – prioritise the highest risk-adjusted expected return per unit of capital (profitability index – BAN-046).

BAN-015.q: Opportunity costs are recorded in the firm's accounting books.
BAN-015.e: False. No transaction occurs, but they must be considered in decisions.
BAN-015.x:
Basis: Decision analysis; VAS 01 (transaction-based recognition).
Analysis: False. Opportunity costs involve no transaction or document → not recorded; but they must be counted in decisions (BAN-002). That's why accounting profit exceeds economic profit (MIC-053).

BAN-016.q: A product sells for 100 at split-off; further processing costs 30 and it then sells for 125. What is the incremental profit from processing further?
BAN-016.e: 125 − 100 − 30 = −5 → sell at split-off; joint costs before split-off are irrelevant.
BAN-016.x:
Basis: Management accounting – sell or process further.
Working: Incremental profit = incremental revenue − further processing cost = (125 − 100) − 30 = 25 − 30 = −5 → sell at the split-off point.
Analysis: Joint costs before split-off are incurred either way → irrelevant. Compare only incremental revenue (25) with incremental cost (30).

BAN-017.q: A project has a 60% chance of earning 500 and 40% chance of losing 200 (VND million). What is the expected value?
BAN-017.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (expected value).
Working: EV = 0.6 × 500 + 0.4 × (−200) = 300 − 80 = VND 220 million.
Analysis: EV is the probability-weighted average – the mean if repeated many times; any single trial yields 500 or −200. Consider the ability to absorb a 200 loss (BAN-018).
Note (investing): this is how Bear/Base/Bull expected returns are computed; pair it with downside analysis.

BAN-018.q: Maximising expected value best suits a decision-maker who is:
BAN-018.e: For one-off, high-stakes decisions, also consider the outcome distribution and capacity to bear losses.
o: Highly risk-averse, facing a one-off ruinous decision
BAN-018.x:
Basis: Decision analysis; von Neumann & Morgenstern (1944) – expected utility theory.
Analysis: Maximising EV suits risk-neutral decision makers and repeated decisions (the law of large numbers makes outcomes converge on EV). For one-off, high-stakes decisions (possible ruin), consider the outcome distribution, worst-case loss and tolerance – use expected utility or maximin (BAN-026).
Distractors: B, C and D don't fit.
Note: Survival > maximum return – don't maximise EV if the downside could cause irrecoverable damage (margin, concentration).

BAN-019.q: Option A: a certain profit of 200. Option B: 50% profit 500, 50% loss 50. What is B's expected value?
BAN-019.x:
Basis: Decision analysis.
Working: EV(B) = 0.5 × 500 + 0.5 × (−50) = 250 − 25 = VND 225 million; EV(A) = 200 (certain).
Analysis: B's EV beats A by 25 but carries risk (standard deviation 275 – BAN-021). The choice depends on risk attitude (BAN-020).

BAN-020.q: Option A: a certain profit of 200. Option B: 50% profit 500, 50% loss 50 (EV 225). A risk-averse decision-maker may choose A despite its lower expected value.
BAN-020.e: True, if their certainty equivalent of B is below 200.
BAN-020.x:
Basis: Expected utility theory (certainty equivalent).
Analysis: True. Risk-averse people have concave utility → B's certainty equivalent (CE) < EV 225. If B's CE < 200 (a risk premium > 25) → choose the certain 200 of A. That's rational, not an error.
Note: Rational risk aversion differs from excessive loss aversion (BAN-080) – e.g., selling a good stock just from fear of short-term volatility.

BAN-021.q: Option B: 50% profit 500, 50% loss 50 (EV 225). What is the standard deviation of outcomes?
BAN-021.x:
Basis: Applied statistics (standard deviation of a discrete variable).
Working: σ² = 0.5 × (500 − 225)² + 0.5 × (−50 − 225)² = 0.5 × 275² + 0.5 × 275² = 75,625 → σ = √75,625 = 275.
Analysis: Coefficient of variation = 275 / 225 ≈ 1.22 – high risk per unit of EV. Standard deviation is symmetric; investors often care more about downside (downside deviation, worst loss −50).

BAN-022.q: Deciding on a plant expansion. Demand is high (p 0.6) or low (0.4). Expand: high 800, low −200. Don't: high 300, low 100. What is the EV of the best option?
BAN-022.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (decision tree – payoff table).
Working: EV(expand) = 0.6 × 800 + 0.4 × (−200) = 480 − 80 = 400; EV(no expansion) = 0.6 × 300 + 0.4 × 100 = 180 + 40 = 220 → expand, EV = VND 400 million.
Analysis: Expanding beats by 180 in EV but risks a 200 loss with low demand (40% probability). A risk-averse decision maker might use maximin (BAN-026) or buy information (BAN-024).

BAN-023.q: Plant expansion: demand high (p 0.6) or low (0.4). Expand: high 800, low −200. Don't: high 300, low 100 (VND million). With perfect advance knowledge of demand, what is the expected value?
BAN-023.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (expected value with perfect information – EVwPI).
Working: Knowing demand is high → expand (800); knowing it's low → don't (100). EVwPI = 0.6 × 800 + 0.4 × 100 = 480 + 40 = VND 520 million.
Analysis: With perfect information you always pick the best option for each state → avoiding the −200 loss in low demand.

BAN-024.q: Plant expansion: demand high (p 0.6) or low (0.4). Expand: high 800, low −200. Don't: high 300, low 100 (VND million). What is the expected value of perfect information (EVPI)?
BAN-024.e: EVPI = 520 − 400 = 120: the most worth paying for any market research.
BAN-024.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (EVPI = EVwPI − best EV without information).
Working: EVPI = 520 − 400 = VND 120 million.
Analysis: 120 million is the most worth paying for any market research – imperfect information is always worth ≤ EVPI (BAN-025, BAN-030).
Check: EVPI = probability of low demand × loss avoided = 0.4 × (100 − (−200)) = 0.4 × 300 = 120 ✓.

BAN-025.q: A market survey costing 150 million isn't worthwhile if EVPI is only 120 million.
BAN-025.e: True. Imperfect information is never worth more than EVPI.
BAN-025.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (EVPI as an upper bound).
Analysis: True. A survey (imperfect information) is worth ≤ EVPI = 120 million (BAN-024); spending 150 million certainly exceeds the maximum possible value → not worth it. The survey's exact value requires EVSI (expected value of sample information) via Bayes (BAN-031).
Note (investing): extra research time and cost also have bounded value – when more information can't change the decision, further research is waste.

BAN-026.q: Payoffs (VND million): Expand – high demand 800, low −200; Don't expand – high 300, low 100. The maximin (pessimistic) criterion picks:
BAN-026.e: Maximin picks the best worst case – suited when losses are unbearable.
BAN-026.x:
Basis: Decision-making under uncertainty (Wald – maximin).
Analysis: Maximin: find each option's worst outcome – expand −200, no expansion 100 → pick the best worst case: no expansion (100 > −200). It suits those who can't absorb losses (weak liquidity, high leverage) or can't estimate probabilities.
Distractors: B is maximax (BAN-027) or EV; C and D are wrong.

BAN-027.q: Payoffs (VND million): Expand – high demand 800, low −200; Don't expand – high 300, low 100. The maximax (optimistic) criterion picks:
BAN-027.x:
Basis: Decision-making under uncertainty (maximax).
Analysis: Maximax: find each option's best outcome – expand 800, no expansion 300 → expand (800). An optimistic rule ignoring loss risk and probabilities – prone to overly risky choices (overconfidence).
Distractors: B is the maximin result; C and D are wrong.

BAN-028.q: Payoffs (VND million): Expand – high demand 800, low −200; Don't expand – high 300, low 100. Under minimax regret, what is the maximum regret of the chosen option?
BAN-028.e: Regrets: Expand (0; 300), Don't (500; 0) → max 300 vs 500 → choose Expand, max regret 300.
BAN-028.x:
Basis: Savage (1951) – minimax regret.
Working: Regret = best payoff in the state − option payoff. High demand (best 800): expand 0, no expansion 500. Low demand (best 100): expand 300, no expansion 0. Maximum regret: expand 300, no expansion 500 → expand, with maximum regret 300.
Analysis: Minimax regret suits decision makers who fear 'missing out' or being judged in hindsight.

BAN-029.e: Clear objectives set the evaluation criteria for later steps.
o: Evaluate, choose and run sensitivity analysis
BAN-029.x:
Basis: Clemen & Reilly – Making Hard Decisions; Hammond, Keeney & Raiffa – Smart Choices (PrOACT).
Analysis: Order: (1) define the problem and objectives (setting evaluation criteria); (2) generate alternatives; (3) identify uncertainties and estimate probabilities; (4) estimate each option's outcomes; (5) evaluate, choose and run sensitivity analysis (BAN-057); (6) implement, monitor and learn (post-mortem).
Note (FERGASITOR): this mirrors First principles → Evidence → Probability → Decision → Execution → Review; a decision journal (BAN-083) records steps 1–5 before outcomes are known.

BAN-030.q: The value of imperfect information (e.g., a sample survey) never exceeds EVPI.
BAN-030.e: True. EVPI is the upper bound on the value of any additional information.
BAN-030.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (EVSI ≤ EVPI).
Analysis: True. Imperfect information (sample surveys, expert forecasts) resolves only part of the uncertainty and can be wrong → its expected value (EVSI) can't exceed that of perfect information (EVPI) – the upper bound on any additional information. Information efficiency = EVSI / EVPI.

BAN-031.q: Prior probability of high demand is 0.6. A survey is 'positive' with probability 0.8 if demand is high and 0.3 if low. Given a positive survey, what is the posterior probability of high demand (%)?
BAN-031.x:
Basis: Bayes' theorem: P(high|+) = P(+|high) × P(high) / P(+).
Working: P(+) = 0.6 × 0.8 + 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.48 + 0.12 = 0.6; P(high|+) = 0.48 / 0.6 = 0.8 = 80%.
Analysis: A positive survey lifts the probability of high demand from 60% (prior) to 80% (posterior). Likewise P(high|−) = 0.6 × 0.2 / 0.4 = 30%.
Note (investing): update beliefs on new evidence in a weighted (Bayesian) way – avoiding both overreaction to short-term news and anchoring on an old thesis.

BAN-032.q: Prior probability of high demand is 0.6. A survey is 'positive' with probability 0.8 if demand is high and 0.3 if low. What is the probability of a positive result (%)?
BAN-032.x:
Basis: Law of total probability.
Working: P(+) = P(+|high) × P(high) + P(+|low) × P(low) = 0.8 × 0.6 + 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.48 + 0.12 = 0.60 = 60%.
Analysis: P(+) is Bayes' denominator (BAN-031) and the branch probability on the decision tree when computing EVSI. 12 points of it are 'false positives' (low demand but a positive survey).

BAN-033.q: In a decision tree, the usual notation is:
BAN-033.e: The tree is solved backwards from right to left (rollback).
o: Squares are decision nodes, circles are chance nodes
BAN-033.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (Raiffa 1968 – decision trees).
Analysis: Convention: squares – decision nodes (the decision maker picks a branch); circles – chance nodes (states of nature with probabilities); end points show payoffs. Solve right to left (rollback): compute EV at circles, choose the highest-EV branch at squares.
Distractors: B, C and D misstate the convention.

BAN-034.q: Select ALL limitations of the expected value method:
BAN-034.e: EV is a long-run average, not a certain outcome.
o: Less meaningful for one-off high-stakes decisions
BAN-034.x:
Basis: Decision analysis; Taleb (2007) – fat tails.
Analysis: EV's limits: (A) it ignores risk attitude (BAN-018, BAN-020); (B) probabilities are often subjective and unverifiable; (C) it means little for one-off, high-stakes decisions; (D) payoff estimates can be biased (optimism, missed tail scenarios).
Distractors: (E) EV is a long-run average, not a certain outcome (no actual payoff may equal it – BAN-019).

BAN-035.q: A project costs 1,000 and returns 400/year for 3 years (year-end); cost of capital 10%. What is NPV (2 decimals)?
BAN-035.x:
Basis: Corporate finance (NPV – Brealey, Myers & Allen).
Working: 3-year, 10% annuity factor = [1 − 1.1⁻³] / 0.1 = (1 − 0.751315) / 0.1 = 2.48685; PV = 400 × 2.48685 ≈ 994.74; NPV = 994.74 − 1,000 ≈ −5.26.
Check: 400/1.1 + 400/1.21 + 400/1.331 = 363.64 + 330.58 + 300.53 = 994.75 ✓.
Analysis: A slightly negative NPV → IRR just under 10% (≈ 9.7%); the project is near economic break-even and very assumption-sensitive.

BAN-036.q: A project costs 1,000 and returns 400/year for 3 years at a 10% cost of capital → NPV ≈ −5.26. The NPV decision is:
BAN-036.e: NPV < 0 destroys value (unless uncounted real options or strategic benefits exist).
BAN-036.x:
Basis: Corporate finance (NPV rule).
Analysis: NPV < 0 (−5.26) → returns below the cost of capital → value-destroying → reject. Exception: real options (expansion, deferral – BAN-064) or unquantified strategic benefits need valuing before deciding.
Distractors: B and C misapply the rule; D – payback doesn't replace NPV (BAN-039).

BAN-037.q: What is the PV of 1,000 received in 2 years at 8% a year (2 decimals)?
BAN-037.x:
Basis: Time value of money: PV = FV / (1 + r)ⁿ.
Working: PV = 1,000 / 1.08² = 1,000 / 1.1664 ≈ 857.34.
Analysis: 1,000 received in 2 years is worth only 857.34 today at 8% – because 857.34 invested today grows to 1,000 in 2 years.
Check: 857.34 × 1.1664 ≈ 1,000 ✓.

BAN-038.q: A project costs 900 with even cash flows of 300/year. What is the simple payback period (years)?
BAN-038.x:
Basis: Corporate finance (payback period).
Working: Payback = investment / annual cash flow = 900 / 300 = 3 years.
Analysis: A simple gauge of how fast capital returns – useful for liquidity risk but with major limits (BAN-039). Discounted payback would exceed 3 years.

BAN-039.q: Simple payback ignores the time value of money and cash flows after payback.
BAN-039.e: True. Use it only as a supplementary liquidity/risk measure.
BAN-039.x:
Basis: Corporate finance.
Analysis: True. Simple payback: (1) ignores the time value of money (a year-3 dong counts like a year-1 dong); (2) ignores cash flows after payback → favouring short projects and possibly rejecting long, high-NPV ones; (3) uses an arbitrary cutoff. Use it only as a liquidity/risk supplement; discounted payback fixes (1) but not (2).

BAN-040.q: The internal rate of return (IRR) is:
BAN-040.e: Accept an independent project if IRR > cost of capital (for conventional cash flows).
o: The discount rate that makes NPV zero
The weighted average cost of capital
BAN-040.x:
Basis: Corporate finance (IRR).
Analysis: IRR is the discount rate making NPV = 0 – the project's internal rate of return. For independent projects with conventional cash flows (one sign change): accept if IRR > cost of capital (same as NPV). Limits: multiple sign changes may give multiple IRRs; mutually exclusive projects may rank differently from NPV (BAN-042).
Distractors: B, C and D are different concepts.

BAN-041.q: Invest 1,000 today and receive 1,210 in exactly 2 years. What is the IRR (%)?
BAN-041.x:
Basis: Corporate finance.
Working: 1,000 × (1 + IRR)² = 1,210 → (1 + IRR) = √1.21 = 1.1 → IRR = 10%.
Check: 1,210 / 1.1² = 1,210 / 1.21 = 1,000 → NPV = 0 ✓.
Analysis: With a single inflow, IRR = (FV/PV)^(1/n) − 1 – equivalent to CAGR. Applications: portfolio CAGR, EPS CAGR (used in PEG = P/E / 5-year CAGR).

BAN-042.q: Two mutually exclusive projects rank differently under NPV and IRR. Choose by:
BAN-042.e: Conflicts arise from scale or timing differences; IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR.
o: Higher NPV, as it directly measures value added for owners
BAN-042.x:
Basis: Corporate finance (Brealey, Myers & Allen – NPV versus IRR).
Analysis: For mutually exclusive projects, when NPV and IRR conflict, choose the higher NPV: it directly measures value added for owners (in money). Conflicts usually stem from scale (a small project with high IRR but low NPV) or timing differences; IRR implicitly assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself – usually unrealistic; NPV assumes reinvestment at the cost of capital.
Distractors: B, C and D don't measure value created.

BAN-043.q: Select ALL relevant cash flows in project appraisal:
BAN-043.e: Prior survey costs are sunk; interest is reflected in the discount rate.
o: Incremental cash flows from the project
Opportunity cost of existing assets used
Survey costs already spent before the decision
BAN-043.x:
Basis: Corporate finance (incremental cash flows).
Analysis: Relevant flows: (A) incremental cash flows (with versus without the project); (B) opportunity cost of existing assets (BAN-002); (C) working capital changes (inventory and receivable build-ups are outflows, recovered at the end); (D) tax effects including depreciation tax shields (BAN-050). Also cannibalisation (BAN-077).
Distractors: (E) Survey costs already spent are sunk; interest is captured in the discount rate (not deducted from cash flows, to avoid double counting).

BAN-044.q: A perpetuity of 50/year at a 10% discount rate. What is its PV?
BAN-044.x:
Basis: Time value of money (perpetuity: PV = C / r).
Working: PV = 50 / 0.10 = 500.
Analysis: Infinite cash flows have finite value because distant flows are worth ever less today. Applications: preferred shares, stable no-growth dividend stocks; P/E = 1/r for a no-growth firm paying out all earnings (e.g., r = 10% → fair P/E 10).

BAN-045.q: Next year's cash flow is 50, growing 3% forever; discount rate 10%. What is the PV (2 decimals)?
BAN-045.x:
Basis: Gordon model (1959) – growing perpetuity: PV = C₁ / (r − g).
Working: PV = 50 / (0.10 − 0.03) = 50 / 0.07 ≈ 714.29.
Analysis: 3% growth lifts value 43% above the no-growth case (500 – BAN-044). The model is very sensitive to (r − g): g = 4% → PV = 833; g = 2% → 625. Conditions: g < r and g sustainable long-term (usually ≤ long-run nominal GDP growth).
Note (valuation): terminal value often dominates DCF totals – be careful with g and Ke (12.63% in the current system).

BAN-046.q: PV of inflows is 1,200 and the initial investment 1,000. What is the profitability index?
BAN-046.e: PI = 1,200/1,000 = 1.2 > 1 → positive NPV; useful under capital rationing.
BAN-046.x:
Basis: Corporate finance (profitability index PI).
Working: PI = PV of inflows / initial investment = 1,200 / 1,000 = 1.2.
Analysis: PI > 1 ⇔ NPV > 0 (NPV = 200). Under capital rationing, rank projects by PI (NPV per unit of capital) to maximise total NPV – like contribution per scarce resource (BAN-014). For mutually exclusive projects without rationing, NPV still rules.

BAN-047.q: A positive-NPV project (with correct cash flows and cost of capital) increases firm value.
BAN-047.e: True. It's a core corporate finance principle.
BAN-047.x:
Basis: Corporate finance (value maximisation).
Analysis: True. A positive NPV means returns above the cost of capital (investors' required return for equivalent risk) → owners gain exactly the NPV. This is the core principle, provided cash flows are estimated correctly and the discount rate reflects project risk.
Note (investing): firms with ROIC durably above WACC create value by reinvesting; with ROIC < WACC, growth destroys value (don't confuse growth with quality growth).

BAN-048.q: Equity 60% (cost 14%), debt 40% (8% pre-tax), CIT 20%. What is WACC (%)?
BAN-048.x:
Basis: Corporate finance (WACC = wE × Ke + wD × Kd × (1 − t)).
Working: WACC = 0.6 × 14% + 0.4 × 8% × (1 − 0.2) = 8.4% + 0.4 × 6.4% = 8.4% + 2.56% = 10.96%.
Analysis: After-tax debt cost is 6.4% because interest is CIT-deductible (tax shield). Weights should be market-value/target structure. The 30%-of-EBITDA interest cap for related-party cases (Decree 132/2020) may shrink the shield.

BAN-049.q: The consistency rule when discounting project cash flows:
o: Discount nominal cash flows at nominal rates and real cash flows at real rates
Always use nominal rates for all flows
BAN-049.x:
Basis: Corporate finance (inflation consistency); Fisher equation.
Analysis: Nominal cash flows (including expected inflation) are discounted at nominal rates; real cash flows (constant prices) at real rates – both give the same NPV if consistent. Mixing (real flows with nominal rates) systematically understates NPV; the reverse inflates it.
Distractors: B, C and D lack consistency.

BAN-050.q: Annual depreciation is VND 200 million and the CIT rate 20%. What is the depreciation tax shield (VND million)?
BAN-050.x:
Basis: Corporate finance (depreciation tax shield); CIT Law (20% standard rate).
Working: Tax shield = depreciation × tax rate = 200 × 20% = VND 40 million.
Analysis: Depreciation isn't a cash outflow but is tax-deductible → tax falls by 40 → cash flow rises 40. Accelerated depreciation (if allowed) brings the shield forward → higher PV. It has value only when the firm has taxable profit.

BAN-051.q: Fixed costs VND 600 million/year; price 200 thousand/unit; variable cost 120 thousand/unit. What is break-even volume (units)?
BAN-051.x:
Basis: Cost–volume–profit (CVP) analysis.
Working: Unit contribution = 200 − 120 = 80 thousand; break-even units = fixed costs / unit contribution = 600,000,000 / 80,000 = 7,500 units.
Check: 7,500 × 80,000 = 600 million = fixed costs ✓.
Analysis: CVP assumptions: constant price, unit variable cost and fixed costs within the relevant range; one product (or a constant mix).

BAN-052.q: Contribution margin ratio 40%, fixed costs VND 600 million. What is break-even revenue (VND million)?
BAN-052.x:
Basis: CVP analysis.
Working: Break-even revenue = fixed costs / contribution margin ratio = 600 / 0.4 = VND 1,500 million.
Analysis: Each unit of revenue contributes 0.4 to fixed costs. Use the CM ratio for multi-product firms (a weighted average by mix).
Check: 1,500 × 40% = 600 ✓.

BAN-053.q: Fixed costs 600 million, contribution 80 thousand/unit. How many units achieve a target profit of 200 million?
BAN-053.x:
Basis: CVP analysis (target volume).
Working: Units = (fixed costs + target profit) / unit contribution = (600 + 200) million / 80 thousand = 800,000,000 / 80,000 = 10,000 units.
Analysis: For an after-tax target, gross up: pre-tax profit = after-tax / (1 − t).
Check: 10,000 × 80,000 − 600 million = 200 million ✓.

BAN-054.q: Expected sales are 10,000 units and break-even 7,500. What is the margin of safety (%)?
BAN-054.x:
Basis: CVP analysis (margin of safety).
Working: Margin of safety = (expected − break-even) / expected = (10,000 − 7,500) / 10,000 = 25%.
Analysis: Sales can fall 25% before losses. Margin of safety × CM ratio = operating margin. It parallels the value-investing 'margin of safety': a buffer against forecast error.

BAN-055.q: Total contribution is 800 and EBIT 200. What is the degree of operating leverage (DOL)?
BAN-055.x:
Basis: CVP analysis (degree of operating leverage – DOL).
Working: DOL = total contribution / EBIT = 800 / 200 = 4.
Analysis: DOL = 1 / margin of safety → margin of safety = 25% (consistent with BAN-054 on the same data). DOL is high with large fixed costs near break-even – EBIT is very revenue-sensitive (BAN-056).

BAN-056.q: DOL = 4. If sales rise 10%, by how much does EBIT rise (%)?
BAN-056.x:
Basis: CVP analysis.
Working: %ΔEBIT = DOL × %ΔRevenue = 4 × 10% = 40%.
Check: Contribution 800 × 1.1 = 880; EBIT = 880 − 600 = 280 = 200 × 1.4 ✓ (fixed costs 600 = 800 − 200).
Analysis: Conversely, revenue −10% → EBIT −40%. With financial leverage (DFL), total leverage DTL = DOL × DFL magnifies EPS further.
Note (cyclicals): high-DOL firms' EPS (steel, airlines) swing hard with the cycle – value them on normalised, not peak, earnings.

BAN-057.e: It identifies key drivers to control or research further.
o: Changing one input at a time (others fixed) to see how results change
Changing several variables together in a consistent story
BAN-057.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis).
Analysis: Sensitivity: change one input at a time (price, volume, cost, discount rate) holding others fixed → see how NPV/profit moves → identify key variables to control or research (tornado chart – BAN-061).
Distractors: B is scenario analysis (BAN-058); C is Monte Carlo (BAN-059); D defeats the purpose.
Note: Limitation – it ignores correlations between variables.

BAN-058.q: Scenario analysis differs from sensitivity analysis in that it:
BAN-058.e: E.g., a recession case: lower price, lower volume and higher rates together.
o: Changes several variables together in consistent cases (bear – base – bull)
BAN-058.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (scenario analysis).
Analysis: Scenarios change several variables together in internally consistent settings (bad – base – good). E.g., a recession: lower prices and volumes, higher rates and NPLs at once – capturing correlations that sensitivity analysis ignores (BAN-057).
Distractors: B is sensitivity; C and D are wrong.
Note (FERGASITOR): probability-weighted Base/Bull/Bear valuations (BAN-060) need each scenario tied to a specific macro–cycle setting.

BAN-059.q: Monte Carlo simulation gives results as a probability distribution (e.g., probability of negative NPV), not a single figure.
BAN-059.e: True. Output quality depends on assumed input distributions and correlations.
BAN-059.x:
Basis: Risk analysis (Monte Carlo simulation – Hertz 1964).
Analysis: True. Monte Carlo assigns probability distributions to inputs and simulates thousands of times → an NPV distribution: expected value, standard deviation, probability of negative NPV, percentiles. Quality depends on the distribution and correlation assumptions ('garbage in, garbage out'); it can create an illusion of precision.

BAN-060.q: Scenario NPVs: bear (25%) −100; base (50%) 200; bull (25%) 500. What is expected NPV?
BAN-060.x:
Basis: Scenario analysis (probability-weighted expected value).
Working: E[NPV] = 0.25 × (−100) + 0.5 × 200 + 0.25 × 500 = −25 + 100 + 125 = VND 200 million.
Analysis: Expected NPV is +200 but there's a 25% chance of −100. Ask: can the firm survive the bad case? Can the downside be reduced (staged investment, abandonment options)? A right-skewed payoff (upside 500 > downside −100) is attractive.
Check: Probabilities 0.25 + 0.5 + 0.25 = 1 ✓.

BAN-061.q: Select ALL good practices in sensitivity/scenario analysis:
o: Focus on the highest-impact variables (tornado chart)
Use realistic ranges based on history
Show break-even values of key variables
Only vary variables that support the desired conclusion
BAN-061.x:
Basis: Decision analysis; Kahneman – confirmation bias.
Analysis: Good practice: (A) focus on the most impactful variables (tornado); (B) ranges based on actual history, not arbitrary ±10%; (C) account for correlations (price and volume often move together over the cycle); (D) show break-even values of key variables (BAN-062) – intuitive for decision makers.
Distractors: (E) Flexing only variables that support the desired conclusion is confirmation bias – defeating the purpose.

BAN-062.q: Base NPV is 200; each 1% fall in price lowers NPV by 50. How far can price fall before NPV hits zero (%)?
BAN-062.x:
Basis: Sensitivity analysis (break-even value of a variable).
Working: Maximum price drop = base NPV / NPV loss per 1% = 200 / 50 = 4%.
Analysis: Prices only 4% below plan wipe out the value → a thin price margin of safety. If historical price swings usually exceed 4% (commodities, materials), the project is risky despite a positive base NPV. Lock in prices (long-term contracts, hedging) or demand a bigger margin.

BAN-063.q: High operating leverage (large fixed costs) amplifies both profits and losses when sales change.
BAN-063.x:
Basis: CVP analysis (operating leverage).
Analysis: True. High fixed costs → high DOL (BAN-055) → rising revenue boosts profit much more, falling revenue magnifies losses. E.g., airlines (aircraft, crews), steel mills (blast furnaces), telecoms (infrastructure): large profit swings over the cycle.
Note (portfolio risk): a high-DOL company with high financial leverage, bought on investor margin, stacks three layers of leverage – a survival risk.

BAN-064.q: The 'option to delay' in project appraisal has value because:
BAN-064.e: Traditional NPV ignores managerial flexibility (real options).
o: Waiting for information avoids investing if the bad scenario occurs
It lowers the cost of capital
BAN-064.x:
Basis: Real options (Myers 1977; Dixit & Pindyck 1994 – Investment under Uncertainty).
Analysis: A deferral option: waiting for information (prices, demand, policy) before irreversible investment → skip investing if the bad case occurs (avoiding loss); invest later if good → more valuable with high uncertainty and irreversibility. Static ('now or never') NPV ignores this flexibility.
Distractors: B – waiting has costs (lost early cash flows, rivals moving first); C and D are wrong.

BAN-065.q: Price elasticity |E| = 4 and marginal cost 30. What is the optimal markup price?
BAN-065.x:
Basis: Managerial economics (markup pricing rule – MIC-072).
Working: P = MC / (1 − 1/|E|) = 30 / (1 − 1/4) = 30 / 0.75 = 40.
Check: Lerner = (40 − 30)/40 = 0.25 = 1/|E| ✓.
Analysis: Elastic demand (|E| = 4) → a low markup (33% over MC). Elasticity can be estimated via log-log regression (BAN-072) or price tests.

BAN-066.e: Penetration pricing suits elastic demand and scale advantages.
o: A new, differentiated product has customers willing to pay high prices and is hard to copy
The market is very price-sensitive and share must be won fast
BAN-066.x:
Basis: Marketing – pricing strategy (Kotler; Dean 1950).
Analysis: Skimming: launch high and cut over time – suits new, differentiated products with buyers willing to pay a premium (initially inelastic demand), barriers to imitation (patents, technology) and limited scale economies. Penetration pricing (low to grab share) suits elastic demand, scale economies and network effects.
Distractors: B, C and D fit penetration or price competition.

BAN-067.q: Contribution margin ratio is 40%. The firm cuts price 10%. What minimum volume increase keeps total contribution unchanged (%, 2 decimals)?
BAN-067.x:
Basis: Management accounting – price-cut analysis.
Working: A 40% CM ratio → price 100, variable cost 60, contribution 40. After a 10% cut: price 90, contribution 30. New volume Q' to keep total contribution: 30 × Q' = 40 × Q → Q' = 1.3333Q → up 33.33%. Formula: ΔP / (CM% − ΔP) = 10 / (40 − 10) = 33.33%.
Analysis: A 10% price cut needs a one-third volume rise just to stand still → discounts are very 'expensive' when margins are thin (BAN-075).

BAN-068.q: Value-based pricing sets price based on customer-perceived value, not just cost.
BAN-068.e: True. Cost is the floor; perceived value is the ceiling.
BAN-068.x:
Basis: Marketing – value-based pricing (Nagle & Müller – The Strategy and Tactics of Pricing).
Analysis: True. Value-based pricing sets prices on customer-perceived value (economic benefit versus the best alternative), not just cost. Cost is the floor (below it, losses), perceived value the ceiling (above it, no purchase); the optimal price lies between, depending on competition.
Note (investing): firms able to price on value (strong brands, high switching costs) earn high, durable margins – a moat signal.

BAN-069.e: Bundles capture extra surplus when customers value components differently.
o: Customers' willingness to pay for the items is negatively correlated
Items are unrelated with very high marginal cost
BAN-069.x:
Basis: Managerial economics (Adams & Yellen 1976 – bundling).
Analysis: Bundling pays when customers' valuations are negatively correlated: customer A values X high and Y low, B the reverse → a bundle priced at each customer's combined valuation captures more surplus than separate sales. E.g., TV packages, office software suites.
Distractors: B – identical valuations make bundling pointless; C – high marginal costs make bundling inefficient (forcing unwanted items); D is wrong.

BAN-070.q: A/B test on a sales page: version A converts 4%, version B 5% (5,000 visits each). What is B's relative uplift over A (%)?
BAN-070.x:
Basis: Data analysis (A/B testing; two-proportion test).
Working: Relative uplift = (5% − 4%) / 4% = 25% (1 point absolute).
Analysis: Test significance: SE of the difference = √[p(1−p)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)] with p ≈ 4.5%, n = 5,000 → ≈ √(0.045 × 0.955 × 0.0004) ≈ 0.41 points; z ≈ 1 / 0.41 ≈ 2.4 > 1.96 → significant at 5%. Don't stop early on attractive interim results (peeking).

BAN-071.q: Using the simple CLV = m/(1 + d − r): annual margin m = VND 2 million, retention r = 80%, discount rate d = 10%. What is CLV (VND million, 2 decimals)?
BAN-071.e: 2/(1 + 0.1 − 0.8) = 2/0.3 ≈ 6.67 million → a ceiling on customer acquisition cost.
BAN-071.x:
Basis: Customer analytics (Gupta & Lehmann 2003 – CLV = m × r/(1 + d − r) or the simple form m/(1 + d − r)).
Working: CLV = m / (1 + d − r) = 2 / (1 + 0.1 − 0.8) = 2 / 0.3 ≈ VND 6.67 million.
Analysis: CLV caps customer acquisition cost (CAC) – CAC > CLV destroys value. It's very retention-sensitive: r = 85% → CLV = 2 / 0.25 = 8 million (+20%).
Note: The formula follows the question; some texts multiply the numerator by r (margins received at period-end).

BAN-072.q: Regressing ln(Q) on ln(P) with controls gives a ln(P) coefficient of −1.8. The correct interpretation:
BAN-072.e: Beware price endogeneity (price and demand driven by common factors) when reading it causally.
o: Estimated price elasticity is −1.8: a 1% price rise cuts quantity by about 1.8%
A 1-dong rise cuts quantity by 1.8 units
BAN-072.x:
Basis: Applied econometrics (log-log model: coefficient = elasticity).
Analysis: In ln(Q) = a + b·ln(P) + …, b = d ln Q / d ln P = price elasticity → b = −1.8: a 1% price rise cuts quantity by about 1.8% (elastic, |E| > 1 → price cuts raise revenue). Beware price endogeneity (price and demand share shocks; firms raise prices when demand is high) → OLS may be biased; use instruments or randomised tests.
Distractors: B interprets a linear model; C and D are wrong.

BAN-073.q: Select ALL factors to consider in pricing decisions:
BAN-073.e: Sunk costs don't affect the optimal price.
BAN-073.x:
Basis: Marketing – pricing (Nagle; the 3C model: Cost – Customer – Competitor).
Analysis: Pricing decisions weigh: (A) variable and incremental costs – the floor; (B) competitors' prices and reactions; (C) customers' willingness to pay – the ceiling (BAN-068); (D) strategic goals (share, premium positioning, penetration).
Distractors: (E) Sunk costs don't affect the optimal price (BAN-003) – demand and marginal cost do.

BAN-074.q: Cost-plus pricing is easy but ignores demand and competitors.
BAN-074.e: True. It may underprice when customers would pay more, or overprice in competitive markets.
BAN-074.x:
Basis: Marketing – cost-plus pricing.
Analysis: True. Cost-plus: price = unit cost × (1 + markup) – easy to apply and explain; drawbacks: it ignores demand and competitors → too low when buyers would pay more (forgone profit) or too high in competitive markets (lost customers); unit cost depends on forecast volume (a spiral: falling sales → higher unit cost → higher price → lower sales).

BAN-075.q: Current price 100, volume 1,000, variable cost 60/unit. Proposal: price 90, expected volume 1,300. How does total contribution change?
BAN-075.x:
Basis: Management accounting – price-cut analysis (BAN-067).
Working: Current contribution = (100 − 60) × 1,000 = 40,000. Proposed: (90 − 60) × 1,300 = 30 × 1,300 = 39,000. Change = 39,000 − 40,000 = −1,000.
Analysis: Volume rises 30%, short of the 33.33% needed (BAN-067: 10/(40 − 10)) → total contribution falls. Price cuts may also trigger rival responses, lifting volume less than planned → don't cut.

BAN-076.q: Pricing at VND 199,000 instead of 200,000 is an example of:
BAN-076.e: It exploits the left-digit effect in price perception.
BAN-076.x:
Basis: Marketing – psychological pricing (Thomas & Morwitz 2005 – left-digit effect).
Analysis: 199,000 versus 200,000: consumers anchor on the left digit → perceiving '100-something' rather than '200' → it seems much cheaper than the real 0.5% difference. This is psychological (odd) pricing.
Distractors: B is individual pricing; C isn't cost-based; D – predatory pricing is selling below cost to eliminate rivals (banned under competition law for dominant firms).

BAN-077.q: When evaluating a new product launch, cannibalisation requires:
BAN-077.e: It follows the incremental cash flow principle.
o: Counting only incremental sales/profit after deducting what's taken from existing products
BAN-077.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (incremental cash flow principle – BAN-043).
Analysis: Cannibalisation: some new-product sales come from customers switching from the firm's own products → count only incremental sales and profit after deducting what the old product loses (BAN-078). But if rivals would take that share anyway, deliberate cannibalisation can still make sense.
Distractors: B, C and D double-count or omit.

BAN-078.q: A new product sells 10,000 units at VND 50 thousand contribution each; 3,000 of these are customers switching from an old product (60 thousand contribution). What is the true incremental contribution (VND million)?
BAN-078.x:
Basis: Decision analysis (cannibalisation).
Working: New-product contribution = 10,000 × 50 = 500 million; lost from the old product = 3,000 × 60 = 180 million; true increment = 500 − 180 = VND 320 million.
Analysis: Switchers move to a lower-margin product (50 < 60) → each switch loses 10 thousand. If switching exceeds plan, benefits shrink fast – run sensitivity on the cannibalisation rate.
Check: 7,000 × 50 + 3,000 × (50 − 60) = 350 − 30 = 320 ✓.

BAN-079.q: Match each bias with an example:
BAN-079.e: Recognising biases is the first step to designing processes that reduce them.
p: Price negotiation driven by the counterparty's first number
Seeking only information that supports the chosen decision
Pouring more money into a losing project because 'too much is invested'
Forecast confidence intervals far too narrow
BAN-079.x:
Basis: Tversky & Kahneman (1974); Kahneman – Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011); Thaler.
Analysis: Anchoring – estimates pulled toward the first number (opening offer, purchase price, old peak). Confirmation bias – seeking only supportive information. Sunk cost fallacy – adding money because 'we've invested so much' (BAN-003). Overconfidence – forecast intervals too narrow.
Note (investment psychology): anchoring on cost, reading only bullish news on holdings, emotional averaging down and overconfident EPS forecasts are the corresponding traps – rules and a decision journal help control them.

BAN-080.e: It explains holding losers too long and selling winners too early (disposition effect).
o: The pain of losing an amount exceeds the pleasure of gaining it (about twice in many studies)
Gains and losses feel the same
BAN-080.x:
Basis: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) – Prospect theory; Tversky & Kahneman (1992) – loss aversion λ ≈ 2.25.
Analysis: Loss aversion: losing hurts more than an equal gain pleases – about twice as much in many studies. The value function is steeper for losses. It explains the disposition effect (Shefrin & Statman 1985): holding losers too long (avoiding realising losses) and selling winners too early.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note: These are exactly the 'taking profits too early' and 'holding because of cost' errors in investment discipline – trend-trailing rules help counter them.

BAN-081.q: Framing effect: the same information presented differently ('90% survive' vs '10% die') can change choices.
BAN-081.e: True. Present decision information in multiple frames.
BAN-081.x:
Basis: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), 'The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice'.
Analysis: True. The same information framed differently changes choices: a gain frame (90% survive) → risk aversion; a loss frame (10% die) → more risk-seeking. Remedy: present information in several frames and convert to common measures (absolute values, probabilities).
Note (investing): 'down 50% from the peak' (a cheapness frame) differs from 'still at 25× P/E' (a valuation frame) – judge on intrinsic value, not price framing.

BAN-082.e: E.g., overestimating a risk after a high-profile incident.
o: Probabilities are judged by how memorable, recent or publicised events are
BAN-082.x:
Basis: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) – 'Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases'.
Analysis: Availability: judging probability by how easily examples come to mind – recent, vivid, heavily covered events are overestimated (air-crash risk after an accident, market crashes after a crisis); less-discussed events are underestimated.
Distractors: B – full statistics are the cure; C is herding; D is the sunk cost fallacy.
Note: Related to recency bias – extrapolating short-term trends.

BAN-083.q: Select ALL techniques that reduce bias in important decisions:
BAN-083.e: Fast gut decisions are most bias-prone.
o: Appointing a devil's advocate or red team
A decision journal recording reasons and assumptions before outcomes
BAN-083.x:
Basis: Klein (2007) – pre-mortem; Kahneman, Lovallo & Sibony (2011) – 'Before You Make That Big Decision'; Tetlock – Superforecasting.
Analysis: Debiasing techniques: (A) pre-mortem – assume failure and find causes; (B) devil's advocates, red teams; (C) a decision journal recording reasons, assumptions and probabilities before outcomes – countering hindsight bias (BAN-090); (D) reference-class forecasting – base rates (BAN-084).
Distractors: (E) Fast intuitive (System 1) decisions are bias-prone.

BAN-084.q: The 'planning fallacy' (projects run late and over budget) is best countered by:
BAN-084.e: The outside view balances the inside view.
o: Reference-class forecasting using actual data from similar projects
BAN-084.x:
Basis: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) – the planning fallacy; Flyvbjerg (2006) – reference-class forecasting.
Analysis: The planning fallacy: the inside view (one's own detailed plan) breeds optimism on cost and timing. The best fix: reference-class forecasting – start from actual outcome distributions of similar projects (e.g., infrastructure overruns averaging 20–45%), then adjust for specifics.
Distractors: B, C and D make it worse.
Note (investing): apply it to company plans (new projects, AGM growth targets) – compare with historical plan-completion rates.

BAN-085.q: Groupthink increases dissenting views in meetings.
BAN-085.e: False. Groupthink suppresses dissent to preserve consensus.
BAN-085.x:
Basis: Janis (1972) – Victims of Groupthink.
Analysis: False. Groupthink: pressure for consensus, illusions of invulnerability, self-censorship and pressure on dissenters → suppressing criticism and degrading decisions (e.g., the Bay of Pigs). Prevention: leaders speak last, appoint devil's advocates, invite outside experts, use anonymous votes.

BAN-086.e: Controls: pre-set stopping rules and independent reviewers.
o: Increasing investment in a failing course to justify earlier decisions
Investing more on positive new evidence
BAN-086.x:
Basis: Staw (1976) – 'Knee-deep in the Big Muddy'.
Analysis: Escalation of commitment: pouring more into a failing course to justify the earlier decision and avoid admitting error – combining the sunk cost fallacy, loss aversion and face-saving. Controls: pre-set exit points (quantitative criteria) and independent reviewers not involved in the original decision.
Distractors: B – positive new evidence is a valid reason; C and D are sound behaviour.
Note (investing): repeatedly averaging down on a stock whose thesis is broken is escalation – hence the rule 'don't average down just because the price fell'.

BAN-087.q: Status quo bias appears when people:
BAN-087.e: Default design (nudges) uses this bias, e.g., auto-enrolment in pensions.
o: Stick with the default even when another option is better
BAN-087.x:
Basis: Samuelson & Zeckhauser (1988) – status quo bias; Thaler & Sunstein (2008) – Nudge.
Analysis: Status quo bias: favouring the default or current option even when another is better – from loss aversion (change feels like loss), switching costs and fear of regret. Default design (nudges) exploits it: automatic pension enrolment sharply raises participation.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the definition.

BAN-088.e: It overstates the effectiveness of strategies and funds.
o: Drawing success lessons only from surviving firms, ignoring bankrupt ones with the same strategy
BAN-088.x:
Basis: Behavioural economics; Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross (1992) – survivorship bias in fund performance.
Analysis: Drawing lessons only from surviving firms, ignoring failures that used the same strategy → overrating the strategy. Likewise, average fund performance is inflated when closed funds are dropped; backtests on today's stock list ignore delisted names.
Distractors: B, C and D are the correct methods to avoid bias.
Note (FERGASITOR system evaluation): backtests of indicators and screens must include delisted stocks.

BAN-089.q: A well-made decision can still have a bad outcome, so evaluation should separate process quality from outcome.
BAN-089.e: True. Judging by outcome alone causes 'outcome bias'.
BAN-089.x:
Basis: Annie Duke (2018) – Thinking in Bets; Baron & Hershey (1988) – outcome bias.
Analysis: True. Outcome = decision quality + luck. A sound process (adequate information, reasonable probabilities, risk management) can still lose to unforeseen events; a poor one can win by luck. Judging by results alone ('resulting') teaches the wrong lessons.
Note: This is the principle of separating process quality from outcome quality in investment reviews.

BAN-090.e: A decision journal shows what was actually known at decision time.
o: Believing after the fact that you knew the outcome all along
BAN-090.x:
Basis: Fischhoff (1975) – 'Hindsight ≠ foresight'.
Analysis: Hindsight bias: after learning the outcome, believing you knew it all along ('I told you so') → overrating predictability, unfairly blaming decision makers and learning the wrong lessons. A decision journal (BAN-083) records what was actually known and the probabilities estimated at the time for comparison.
Distractors: B, C and D are other concepts.

BAN-091.q: Match each SWOT quadrant with its nature:
BAN-091.e: SWOT is useful when turned into combined strategies (SO, WO, ST, WT).
BAN-091.x:
Basis: Strategic analysis (Andrews 1971; Weihrich 1982 – TOWS matrix).
Analysis: Strengths (S) – internal, positive (brand, low cost). Weaknesses (W) – internal, negative (high debt, weak governance). Opportunities (O) – external, positive (public investment, market upgrade). Threats (T) – external, negative (rising rates, new rivals). SWOT is useful when turned into SO, WO, ST and WT strategies, not just lists.

BAN-092.q: Select ALL forces in Porter's Five Forces model:
BAN-092.e: The exchange rate is a macro (PESTEL) factor, not one of the five forces.
BAN-092.x:
Basis: Porter (1979), 'How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy', Harvard Business Review.
Analysis: The five forces: (A) rivalry among existing firms; (B) threat of new entrants (barriers – MIC-069); (C) supplier bargaining power; (D) buyer bargaining power; (E) threat of substitutes. Weaker forces → higher long-run industry profitability.
Distractors: (F) Exchange rates are a macro (PESTEL) factor with indirect effects.
Note: Step 2 (industry analysis) of the stock screening process.

BAN-093.q: Per BABOK v3 (IIBA), business analysis is:
BAN-093.e: Its core concept model: change, need, solution, stakeholder, value, context.
o: The practice of enabling change by defining needs and recommending solutions that deliver value to stakeholders
BAN-093.x:
Basis: IIBA – BABOK Guide v3 (2015), chapter 2 (Business Analysis Core Concept Model – BACCM).
Analysis: Business analysis enables change in an enterprise by defining needs and recommending solutions that deliver value to stakeholders. The BACCM has six concepts: change, need, solution, stakeholder, value, context.
Distractors: B is development; C is auditing; D – documentation is only part of the work.

BAN-094.q: The MoSCoW prioritisation technique classifies requirements as:
BAN-094.e: It helps agree scope under limited resources and time.
o: Must have – Should have – Could have – Won't have (this time)
BAN-094.x:
Basis: IIBA – BABOK Guide v3 (prioritisation technique – 10.33); Clegg (DSDM, 1994).
Analysis: MoSCoW: Must have (essential – without it the solution fails); Should have (important but with a workaround); Could have (desirable if resources allow); Won't have this time (excluded for now). It aligns scope when time and resources are limited.
Distractors: B is an investment recommendation; C is SWOT; D are other criteria.
Note: Useful when specifying Pine Script requirements – settle Must-haves (MACD signals, request.security limits) before adding features.

BAN-095.q: Arrange the root cause analysis process for an operational problem (e.g., rising late deliveries):
BAN-095.e: Skipping verification tends to fix symptoms instead of causes.
o: Define the problem and measure the baseline
Verify the root cause with data and 5 Whys
BAN-095.x:
Basis: IIBA – BABOK Guide v3 (root cause analysis – 10.40); Ishikawa (fishbone); Ohno (5 Whys); DMAIC.
Analysis: Order: (1) define the problem and measure the baseline (8% late, since when, where); (2) gather relevant data; (3) list potential causes (fishbone: people, machines, methods, materials, measurement, environment); (4) verify root causes with data and 5 Whys; (5) implement solutions and re-measure.
Note: Skipping verification tends to fix symptoms rather than causes (FRD-070, ICA-097).

BAN-096.q: Good objectives and requirements should be SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound.
BAN-096.e: True. E.g., 'cut late deliveries from 8% to 3% by 31/12'.
BAN-096.x:
Basis: Doran (1981) – SMART goals; management by objectives (Drucker 1954).
Analysis: True. SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. 'Cut late deliveries from 8% to 3% by 31 Dec' meets all criteria; 'improve delivery' doesn't (ICA-016).
Note: Investment goals should be SMART too – e.g., yearly capital targets, margin limits, minimum cash levels.

BAN-097.q: In Porter's value chain, the primary activities are:
BAN-097.e: HR, technology, procurement and infrastructure are support activities.
o: Inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service
BAN-097.x:
Basis: Porter (1985) – Competitive Advantage (value chain).
Analysis: Primary activities: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service. Support activities: HR management, technology development, procurement, firm infrastructure (finance, accounting, legal, general management). Advantage comes from how activities are performed and linked.
Distractors: B are support activities; C belong to firm infrastructure (support); D is incomplete.

BAN-098.q: The Pareto (80/20) principle in business analysis suggests:
BAN-098.e: Exact ratios vary; it's a rule of thumb for focus.
o: A few causes, customers or products usually drive most results, so prioritise resources
BAN-098.x:
Basis: Pareto (1896); Juran (1951) – 'the vital few and the trivial many'.
Analysis: The 80/20 rule: a few causes, customers or products drive most results (e.g., 20% of customers give 80% of revenue; a few defects cause most complaints) → focus resources on the vital few. Exact ratios vary; it's a rule of thumb for focus (Pareto charts).
Distractors: B, C and D misread it.
Note: In portfolios, a few big decisions (core positions, leverage) drive most results – concentrate discipline there.

BAN-099.q: Weighted supplier scoring: price 40%, quality 35%, delivery 25%. Supplier X scores 7, 9, 8. What is the weighted score?
BAN-099.x:
Basis: Multi-criteria analysis (weighted scoring model).
Working: Score = 0.4 × 7 + 0.35 × 9 + 0.25 × 8 = 2.8 + 3.15 + 2.0 = 7.95.
Analysis: Results are weight-sensitive – agree weights before scoring (no tweaking to reach a desired answer), test sensitivity, and set knock-out thresholds for must-have criteria (e.g., quality < 6 disqualifies despite a high total).
Check: Weights 0.4 + 0.35 + 0.25 = 1 ✓.

BAN-100.q: On a stakeholder power–interest grid, the 'high power, high interest' group should be:
BAN-100.e: High power–low interest: keep satisfied; low power–high interest: keep informed.
o: Managed closely, consulted and involved in decisions
BAN-100.x:
Basis: IIBA – BABOK Guide v3 (stakeholder analysis – 10.43); Mendelow (1991) – power–interest grid.
Analysis: Four groups: high power – high interest: manage closely, consult and co-decide (key players); high power – low interest: keep satisfied; low power – high interest: keep informed; low power – low interest: monitor.
Distractors: B, C and D suit less important groups; applying them to key players endangers the project.
